## Appendix A Impact of the SRT source terms on energy spectra

The impact of the SRT source terms (12–13) on the energy spectra is examined. Combining (7) and (9), the momentum equation can be written as

$$ \frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial s}=-u_{j}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}-\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x_{i}}-\frac{\partial\tau_{ij}}{\partial x_{j}}\right)+\frac{y}{\tau_{0}}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial y}-\frac{u_{i}}{2\tau_{0}}. $$

Applying a Fourier transform (notated as $\mathcal{F}$ ) to (58) in the homogeneous directions ( $x$ , $z$ ) yields

$$ \frac{\partial\hat{u}_{i}}{\partial s}=\mathcal{F}\left[-u_{j}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}-\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x_{i}}-\frac{\partial\tau_{ij}}{\partial x_{j}}\right)\right]+\frac{y}{\tau_{0}}\frac{\partial\hat{u}_{i}}{\partial y}-\frac{\hat{u}_{i}}{2\tau_{0}}, $$

where $\hat{u}_{i}=\mathcal{F}(u_{i})$ , and the in-plane Fourier transform commutes with the differential operator in $y$ . Then, (59) is multiplied by $\hat{u}_{i}^{*}$ to derive an equation for the two-dimensional energy spectra $\hat{E}(k_{x},y,k_{z},s)=(\hat{u}_{i}\hat{u}_{i}^{*})/2$ . The result is

$$ \frac{\partial\hat{E}}{\partial s}=\hat{u}_{i}^{*}\cdot\mathcal{F}\left[-u_{j}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}-\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x_{i}}-\frac{\partial\tau_{ij}}{\partial x_{j}}\right)\right]+\frac{1}{\tau_{0}}\left(y\frac{\partial}{\partial y}-1\right)\hat{E}. $$

Represented by the rightmost term in (60), the source terms act proportionally to the in-plane TKE spectra, and do not selectively inject or remove energy in any specific wavenumber range. Graphically, the effect of the source terms corresponds to a continuous downward shift of the entire energy spectra (when displayed on a logarithmic scale).

## Appendix B Analytical solution to variable-density one-dimensional diffusion

The one-dimensional variable-density temporal diffusion problem in $(t,y)$ coordinates is entirely governed by continuity, scalar transport, and the equation of state. They are

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial\rho v}{\partial y}=0, \displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho Y}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial\rho vY}{\partial y}=D\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\rho\frac{\partial Y}{\partial y}\right), \displaystyle\rho(Y)=\frac{\rho_{H}\rho_{L}}{\rho_{H}-Y\Delta\rho}. $$

Equations (61)–(63) determine $\rho$ , $v$ , and $Y$ completely. The solution is diffusion driven and does not depend on gravity. With $\rho$ and $v$ determined, the pressure can be obtained from the momentum equation using known values of $g$ and $\nu$ .

The analytical self-similar solution to the variable-density diffusion problem, expressed in terms of the similarity variable, $\zeta=y/\sqrt{4Dt}=y/h_{D}$ , (notated with subscript $D$ for “diffusion”), is

$$ \displaystyle X=\frac{\rho-\rho_{L}}{\Delta\rho}=\frac{1}{2}(1+\erf\zeta), \displaystyle\frac{\rho v}{\Delta\rho D/h_{D}}=-\frac{{\rm d}X}{{\rm d}\zeta}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-\zeta^{2}}, $$

where the solution for the mole fraction is identical to that of the constant-density problem, and variable-density effects are only observed in the velocity. The mole fraction $X$ is solely a function of $\zeta$ and independent of the reservoir densities. In contrast, the mass fraction $Y$ , which is algebraically related to $X$ by the equation of state, $Y(X,R)=RX/[1+(1-R)X]$ , does vary with the density ratio (i.e. Atwood number). By extension, this is generally true for all functions of $Y$ , including the one-dimensional mixed mass, $m=\rho Y(1-Y)$ , and scalar dissipation rate, $\chi=2\rho D(\partial Y/\partial y)^{2}$ , as shown in figure 16. For ease of comparison with the SRT results, quantities in figure 16 are normalized with the equivalent variables, where $h_{1}=\sqrt{8/\pi}h_{D}$ , $M=\int\rho m\,{\rm d}y$ , and $\tau_{0}=h_{D}/\dot{h}_{D}=h_{D}^{2}/2D=\pi h_{1}^{2}/16D$ . As $A$ increases, the mass fraction and velocity shifts leftwards, the mixed mass profile broadens with a reduction in its peak value, and the scalar dissipation narrows while experiencing an increase in its peak value.

## Appendix C Closure equation for $h_{1}$

To derive a time evolution equation for the instantaneous mixing layer height $h_{1}(s)$ , density is written in terms of the mole fraction, $\rho=\rho_{L}+\Delta\rho X$ , and substituted into the continuity equation to yield

$$ \frac{\partial\langle X\rangle_{1,3}}{\partial s}+\frac{1}{\Delta\rho}\frac{\partial\langle\rho v\rangle_{1,3}}{\partial y}=\frac{y}{\tau_{0}}\frac{\partial\langle X\rangle_{1,3}}{\partial y}. $$

An equation for the transport of $\langle X\rangle_{1,3}^{2}$ is obtained by multiplying (66) with $2\langle X\rangle_{1,3}$ to get

$$ \frac{\partial\langle X\rangle_{1,3}^{2}}{\partial s}+\frac{2}{\Delta\rho}\langle X\rangle_{1,3}\frac{\partial\langle\rho v\rangle_{1,3}}{\partial y}=\frac{y}{\tau_{0}}\frac{\partial\langle X\rangle_{1,3}^{2}}{\partial y}. $$

Combining (66) and (67) results in

$$ \frac{{\rm d}h_{1}}{{\rm d}s}=\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\int 4\left(\langle X\rangle_{1,3}-\langle X\rangle_{1,3}^{2}\right)\,{\rm d}y=\frac{8}{\Delta\rho}\int\langle X\rangle_{1,3}\frac{\partial\langle\rho v\rangle_{1,3}}{\partial y}\,{\rm d}y-\frac{h_{1}}{\tau_{0}}. $$

The SRT parameter $\tau_{0}$ is implemented by assuming a stationary solution, $dh_{1}/ds=0$ , to (68) and substituting $h_{1}=\hat{h}_{1}$ so that

$$ \frac{1}{\tau_{0}(s)}=\frac{8}{\Delta\rho\hat{h}_{1}}\int\langle X\rangle_{1,3}\frac{\partial\langle\rho v\rangle_{1,3}}{\partial y}\,{\rm d}y. $$

Substituting (69) into (68) results in a time evolution equation for $h_{1}$ that is written as

$$ \frac{{\rm d}h_{1}}{{\rm d}s}=\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\int 4\langle X\rangle_{1,3}\left(1-\langle X\rangle_{1,3}\right)\,{\rm d}y=\left[\frac{8}{\Delta\rho}\int\langle X\rangle_{1,3}\frac{\partial\langle\rho v\rangle_{1,3}}{\partial y}\,{\rm d}y\right]\left(1-\frac{h_{1}}{\hat{h}_{1}}\right). $$

The integral factor in the RHS of (70) is positive for an unstable RT flow configuration, hence the use of (69) results in a stable relaxation equation for $h_{1}$ . The use of closure equations such as (14) or (69) (as opposed to a constant $\tau_{0}$ ) is simply a practical way of achieving a specified mixing layer height without the need to guess the value of $\tau_{0}$ a priori. It was shown in Appendix A of Goh and Blanquart (2025) that the ensemble dynamics of SRT flow is equivalent for different implementations of $\tau_{0}$ as long as the value of the time average $\bar{\tau}_{0}$ is the same.

## Appendix D Local scaling of turbulent kinetic energy with buoyancy production

A qualitative observation about the TKE budget profiles in figures 5 and 6 is that buoyancy production and TKE profiles have similar shapes that resemble a Gaussian function. To assess their similarities more quantitatively, buoyancy production is normalized by TKE and shown in figure 17. Towards the edge of the mixing layer, both buoyancy production and TKE approach 0, and the division of small values may lead to significant noise. To focus on the behavior of the bulk of the mixing layer, only regions where buoyancy production is at least 10% of its maximum value are shown.

The normalized ratio of buoyancy production to TKE growth is remarkably constant across the mixing layer at around 2.2, which suggests that the buoyancy production scaling applies not only globally, but also locally, and that the TKE profile largely preserves the shape of buoyancy production (and by extension, the mean mass flux). This local scaling of TKE with buoyancy production is a key observation that is utilized in the derivation of the scaling for $\tau_{0}$ in § 4.2.

# Thermal laser evaporation of superconducting Nb films

**Authors:** Yifei Yan Affiliation: Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA David S. Minnich Email: aminnich@caltech.edu Affiliation: Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA

## Abstract

Thermal laser evaporation (TLE) is an emerging physical vapor deposition (PVD) technique that uses continuous-wave lasers to evaporate even the most refractory elements. The deposition and characterization of superconducting refractory elements are of interest to assess the quality of films deposited by TLE. Here, we report the deposition of niobium (Nb) on c-plane sapphire using a home-built TLE system equipped with a 1070 nm continuous-wave fiber laser. A deposition rate of 0.19 Å/s was achieved with 533 W of laser power focused to a diameter of approximately 500 µm on a Nb target. A film with a thickness of $22.47\pm 0.05$ nm and a root-mean-square (RMS) roughness of $0.23\pm 0.02$ nm exhibited a room-temperature resistivity of $21.60\pm 0.05$ µ $\Omega\mathrm{cm}$ and a residual-resistivity ratio (RRR) of 5.71. The superconducting transition temperature, $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , of the film was measured as 9.24 K, only 10 mK below the bulk value, with a transition width of 29 mK. Among films deposited without substrate heating, the electrical and superconducting properties of the present films meet or exceed those deposited by other techniques. This work contributes to the emerging consensus regarding TLE as a versatile PVD method for refractory elements and compounds.

## Introduction

Niobium (Nb) is a refractory transition metal with the highest bulk superconducting transition temperature, $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , of 9.25 K among all elemental superconductors [39]. Its low quasiparticle loss at accessible temperatures below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ [34] and well-established thin-film growth techniques [12, 26, 42, 11, 2, 32] have made it an important material for superconducting electronics. In thin-film form, Nb is widely employed in superconducting microwave resonators [40], Josephson junctions [35], and transmon qubits[3], where device performance is sensitive to the superconducting properties and microstructure, as well as the quality of the surfaces and interfaces of the film [1, 8, 28].

Nb films are commonly prepared by sputtering and electron-beam evaporation, both of which have produced superconducting films suitable for device fabrication [30, 22]. In sputtering, plasma-generated energetic species and gas-phase collisions introduce additional kinetic parameters that influence film microstructure and residual stress [41]. Electron-beam evaporation enables thermal evaporation of refractory materials but introduces additional process complexity. Electron-beam sources exhibit flux instabilities and therefore may require active monitoring and feedback control [6]. For refractory metals, achieving sufficiently high vapor fluxes for deposition requires high source temperatures and beam powers, necessitating the consideration of source containment, crucible compatibility, and contamination control [25]. In addition, secondary and backscattered electrons as well as ionized vapor species generated during evaporation can interfere with lithographic processing, causing deposition beneath resist undercuts, resist damage, and lift-off defects [37].

Thermal laser evaporation (TLE) is an emerging physical vapor deposition (PVD) technique that uses continuous-wave lasers to heat a localized region of a source, producing vapor for deposition. The surrounding material outside of the irradiated region can remain solid, allowing many elements to be evaporated from free-standing sources without crucibles, while the evaporation rate can be adjusted through the incident laser power. Unlike sputtering, TLE does not require a process plasma, providing a comparatively simple environment for film growth. It also avoids the complexities associated with electron-beam evaporation such as contamination from the crucible. TLE has been demonstrated for nonradioactive solid elements across the periodic table [32] and has subsequently enabled the growth of epitaxial films of elemental and compound materials [24, 21, 20, 18], including superconducting $\alpha$ -Ta [24] and TiN [18]. Epitaxial oxide and nitride films have been grown in oxygen/ozone mixtures and ammonia at pressures up to around $10^{-3}$ Torr. [21, 18]. Recently, we reported nickel deposition using a home-built TLE system [5]. However, the properties of Nb films deposited by TLE have not been reported.

Here, we report the deposition and characterization of Nb films on c-plane sapphire substrates using TLE. The thin films were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), atomic force microscopy (AFM), room-temperature van der Pauw (vdP) measurements, and temperature-dependent electrical transport. Two films deposited under nominally identical conditions exhibited reproducible properties; the film with the highest superconducting transition temperature exhibited $T_{\mathrm{c}}=9.24$ K and a residual-resistivity ratio (RRR) of 5.71 with a thickness of $22.47\pm 0.05$ nm. The present films exhibit near-bulk $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ and RRR values approximately 1.5–2.5 times those reported for Nb films of comparable thickness deposited using conventional techniques without substrate heating. This work indicates that TLE is a promising technique for deposition of superconducting refractory compounds.

## Experimental Methods

### Film deposition

Nb thin films were deposited on c-plane sapphire substrates (MTI Corporation, c-plane, $10\times 10\times 0.5$ mm, single-side polished) using the home-built TLE system described in our previous work [5]. Briefly, the system consists of a water-cooled ultrahigh-vacuum (UHV) chamber equipped with bellows-mounted target and substrate holders and a laser-delivery system, consisting of a fiber-laser coupler, collimator, and focusing optics. The laser is directed through a flange-mounted window onto the target using a water-cooled off-axis mirror. A continuous-wave 1070 nm fiber laser serves as the heating source. The target is press-fit into a molybdenum holder, with a type-C thermocouple positioned beneath it. The thermocouple serves primarily as a safety indicator to confirm the laser is hitting the target; its readings are not used to quantify the evaporation-surface temperature. The reflected laser beam is intercepted by a water-cooled beam dump.

In this work, a free-standing Nb target (Thermo Scientific, 99.95%) was heated by the laser to generate the evaporation flux. Several changes were made compared to our prior deposition of Ni. [5] First, the beam was focused more tightly to a diameter of approximately 500 µm to achieve a higher power density. Second, we observed changes in the target surface morphology caused by prolonged localized laser heating at a fixed position, as has been reported previously [33]. These variations lead to flux instabilities. We addressed this problem by rastering the laser beam across the target surface, limiting localized deformation and helping to preserve the evaporation geometry and flux distribution during deposition. A similar strategy is used in pulsed-laser deposition to reduce localized target modification and promote uniform ablation [13].

Another origin of flux instability is a change in mirror reflectivity caused by material deposition. An increase in the laser power required to maintain the deposition rate was initially observed, consistent with a decrease in mirror reflectivity caused by Nb deposition. This effect plateaued after several deposition runs, after which a reproducible growth rate could be achieved at a fixed laser power.

Before deposition, the chamber was evacuated to a base pressure of $2\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{Torr}$ , determined by an Edwards nWRG digital gauge. The Nb target and its holder were baked out at a laser power of 375 W. A residual gas analyzer (SRS RGA200) was used to evaluate the chamber vacuum condition. Desorbing water vapor was detected, and the deposition did not start until the partial pressure of the water dropped below $10^{-8}\,\mathrm{Torr}$ . To reduce surface organic contamination, the as-received sapphire substrates were immersed in freshly prepared piranha solution ( $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}:30\%~\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}=3:1$ by volume) for 30 s and subsequently rinsed with deionized water. They were then mounted approximately 8 cm from the Nb target and held under vacuum overnight at room temperature before deposition. During deposition, the hydrogen partial pressure was observed to exceed $5\times 10^{-7}$ Torr, consistent with the well-known affinity of Nb for hydrogen [4]. The substrates were not heated. No substrate rotation was employed. To begin deposition, the laser power was increased to 533 W and the substrate shutter was removed. The deposition was performed for 20 min. The film thickness was measured by X-ray reflectivity (XRR) performed with a step size of $0.002^{\circ}$ and a scan speed of $1^{\circ}$ /min. The average deposition rate was obtained by dividing the measured thickness by the deposition time.

### Surface and structural characterization

Surface morphology was characterized by a Bruker Dimension Icon AFM in PeakForce tapping mode using a ScanAsyst-Air probe over scan areas of 500 nm $\times$ 500 nm. The images were processed using NanoScope Analysis, with first-order flattening applied to remove scanner background. The root-mean-square (RMS) surface roughness, $R_{\mathrm{q}}$ , was calculated over the scan area.

XRD measurements were performed using a Rigaku Smartlab diffractometer with a Cu-K $\alpha_{1}$ source. Symmetric $\theta$ – $2\theta$ scans were collected with a step size of $0.02^{\circ}$ and a scan speed of $2.4^{\circ}$ /min. Diffraction peaks were assigned by comparison with reference patterns for body-centered cubic (bcc) Nb and c-plane sapphire. The out-of-plane coherent domain size was estimated from the measured Nb peak width using the Scherrer equation without correction for instrumental broadening.

### Electrical transport measurements

Room-temperature sheet resistance was measured using the vdP method with four electrical contacts positioned near the sample perimeter by aluminum (Al) wire bonding using a TPT HB05 wire bonder. Measurements were performed in both reciprocal contact configurations with a Keithley 2400 SourceMeter using an excitation current of $10\text{\,}\mathrm{mA}$ . The film resistivity, $\rho$ , was calculated as $\rho=R_{\mathrm{s}}t$ , where $R_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the measured sheet resistance and $t$ is the film thickness.

Temperature-dependent electrical resistivity was measured using a Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS, Quantum Design DynaCool) in a four-probe configuration with an excitation current of $100\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro A}$ . The sample was cooled from 300 to 20 K at 10 K/min, from 20 to 9.5 K at 1 K/min, from 9.5 to 8.5 K at 0.5 K/min, and from 8.5 to 2 K at 1 K/min. Measurements were acquired at nominal temperature intervals of 1, 0.05, 0.01, and 0.05 K over these respective ranges.

## Results

Two Nb films, denoted samples A and B, were deposited in separate runs under nominally identical conditions to assess the run-to-run reproducibility of the TLE system. The figures show the measured properties for sample A, while the corresponding properties of sample B are reported in the text for comparison.

*Figure 1: Structural characterization of sample A. (a) XRR versus angle (black line) and the corresponding GenX fit (red line), yielding a film thickness of $22.47\pm 0.05$ nm. (b,c) Symmetric $\theta$ – $2\theta$ XRD scans over different angular ranges using Cu-K $\alpha_{1}$ radiation. The diffraction peaks at $38.553\pm 0.003^{\circ}$ and $111.494\pm 0.005^{\circ}$ are assigned to Nb(110) and Nb(222), respectively. Asterisks (*) denote reflections from the c-plane sapphire substrate.*

Figure 1 shows the XRR profile of sample A. The experimental data were fitted using GenX [14], employing a multilayer model consisting of air/Nb2O5/Nb/sapphire. The fitted thicknesses of the Nb and Nb2O5 layers were $19.77\pm 0.05$ nm and $2.70\pm 0.05$ nm, respectively, yielding a total film thickness of $22.47\pm 0.05$ nm. The thickness uncertainties were estimated from the parameter ranges corresponding to a 5% increase in the minimum logarithmic figure of merit (FOM). Throughout this work, the term “film thickness” refers to the total thickness, including the oxide layer. The observed Kiessig fringes are consistent with well-defined interfaces and a relatively uniform film thickness. Based on the fitted total thickness and deposition time, the deposition rate was calculated to be approximately 0.19 Å/s. The corresponding thicknesses of the Nb and Nb2O5 layers and the total film thickness of sample B were $20.63\pm 0.11$ nm, $2.21\pm 0.07$ nm, and $22.84\pm 0.07$ nm, respectively, yielding a deposition rate of 0.19 Å/s. The deposition rates obtained in this study are close to the rate reported for electron-beam evaporation of Nb for device fabrication [22, 27]. Previous TLE work reported a rate of approximately 0.34 Å/s at 250 W (ref. [33]), whereas the present growth rate was lower even at a higher laser power, likely because the larger target size and press-fit mounting design of our system resulted in larger radiative and conductive heat losses. Higher deposition rates could be achieved by increasing the laser power or reducing the target size and its thermal coupling to the holder.

The $\theta$ – $2\theta$ XRD pattern of sample A is shown in Figures 1 and 1. The diffraction peaks were fitted using a pseudo-Voigt line shape to extract the peak position $2\theta$ and the full width at half maximum of the diffraction peak $\beta$ (in radians). Their uncertainties represent one standard error, calculated from the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix of the least-squares fit. In addition to reflections from the c-plane sapphire substrate, peaks assigned to bcc Nb(110) and Nb(222) are observed at $2\theta=$ $38.553\pm 0.003^{\circ}$ and $111.494\pm 0.005^{\circ}$ , respectively. Relative to the bulk reference positions of $38.545^{\circ}$ and $107.897^{\circ}$ , these shifts correspond to out-of-plane compressive strains of $(-0.020\pm 0.007)\%$ and $(-2.186\pm 0.003)\%$ , respectively, as calculated using Bragg’s law. The strain uncertainties were propagated from the fitted peak-position uncertainties, treating the bulk reference positions as exact. The substantial compression inferred for the Nb[111]-oriented component remains unexplained, and further structural characterization is needed to confirm the origin of the peak shift.

The out-of-plane coherent domain size was estimated using the Scherrer equation,

$$ D=\frac{K\lambda}{\beta\cos\theta}, $$

where $D$ is the coherent domain size, $K$ is the Scherrer shape factor, and $\lambda$ is the X-ray wavelength. Using $K=0.9$ and $\lambda=1.5406~\text{\AA}$ for Cu-K $\alpha_{1}$ radiation, the resulting coherent domain sizes were $18.77\pm 0.40$ nm for Nb(110) and $8.70\pm 0.10$ nm for Nb(222). The uncertainties were propagated from the fitted $\beta$ and $\theta$ , accounting for their covariance. These values describe the diffraction coherence length normal to the corresponding lattice planes.

It is well established that substrate temperature can strongly influence thin-film texture and preferred crystallographic orientation, and Nb grown on c-plane sapphire is no exception. Drimmer et al. observed a temperature-driven evolution from predominantly Nb[110]-oriented growth toward Nb[111]-oriented growth as the substrate temperature was increased to 975 K [10]. At even higher temperatures, Wagner reported the opposite orientation transition, with Nb{111} parallel to the sapphire basal plane at $900\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and Nb{110} at $1100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ [38]. These results highlight the strong dependence of Nb orientation on the specific growth conditions. However, the relatively strong Nb(222) reflection observed here is still unexpected based on previous studies [31, 10, 7]. A possible contributor to the observed Nb(222) reflection is the absence of substrate rotation during deposition. Without rotation, the local incidence angle of the incoming vapor flux varies across the substrate and is not azimuthally averaged during growth. This spatially varying deposition geometry may alter the local growth kinetics and, consequently, the preferred crystallographic orientation across the film.

An additional diffraction peak was observed at $44.343\pm 0.008^{\circ}$ , which could not be assigned to a Bragg reflection of bcc Nb. A separate XRD scan of the bare aluminum sample plate confirmed that this peak originates from the sample plate. Sample B also exhibits the same Nb(110) and Nb(222) reflections, with corresponding Bragg peaks at $38.512\pm 0.010^{\circ}$ and $110.972\pm 0.006^{\circ}$ , and coherent domain sizes of $19.99\pm 1.55$ nm and $5.37\pm 0.04$ nm, respectively. Relative to the same bulk reference positions, these peak shifts correspond to an out-of-plane tensile strain of $(0.082\pm 0.025)\%$ for the Nb[110]-oriented component and a compressive strain of $(-1.881\pm 0.004)\%$ for the Nb[111]-oriented component.

*Figure 2: AFM topography of sample A over a 500 nm $\times$ 500 nm scan area. The RMS surface roughness is $R_{q}=0.23\pm 0.02$ nm, where the uncertainty represents the standard deviation of the roughness values calculated from individual line scans. The image was processed using NanoScope Analysis with first-order flattening applied. The color scale represents surface height in nanometers.*

Figure 2 shows an AFM topographic image of sample A over a 500 nm $\times$ 500 nm area. The film exhibits a smooth and uniform surface within the scanned region, with an RMS roughness, $R_{\mathrm{q}}=0.23\pm 0.02$ nm. Sample B has a comparable $R_{\mathrm{q}}=0.28\pm 0.03$ nm. The uncertainty represents the standard deviation of the roughness values calculated from individual line scans. This low surface roughness is consistent with the pronounced Kiessig fringes observed by XRR, whose visibility indicates smooth surface and buried interfaces, together with good thickness uniformity across the X-ray-illuminated area. The AFM and XRR data therefore provide complementary evidence for the smoothness and uniformity of the film.

*Figure 3: (a) Measured electrical resistivity versus temperature. The inset shows a magnified view of the superconducting transition region. The dashed line is a guide to the eye. (b) Superconducting transition temperature of Nb thin films versus thickness from this work (filled red squares) and other techniques including DC magnetron sputtering in Ref. 31 (open purple diamonds), Ref. 16 (open blue circles), Ref. 43 (open grey triangles), and Ref. 29 (open yellow squares), and e-beam evaporation in Ref. 27 (open green pentagons).*

*Figure 4: (a) Room-temperature resistivity, (b) superconducting transition width, and (c) RRR versus thickness from this work (filled red squares) and previous studies. Data from Ref. 29 (open yellow squares), Ref. 43 (open grey triangles), and Ref. 27 (open green pentagons) are also shown for comparison.*

Figure 3 shows the temperature-dependent resistivity of sample A. The raw resistance data were calibrated with respect to the room-temperature resistivity, $\rho_{\mathrm{300}}=21.60\pm 0.05$ µ $\Omega\mathrm{cm}$ , calculated from the sheet resistance measured by the standard vdP method and the thickness characterized by XRR. The reported resistivity uncertainty was propagated from the XRR thickness uncertainty, neglecting uncertainty in the measured sheet resistance. For reference, the bulk resistivity of Nb is 15.2 µ $\Omega\mathrm{cm}$ at 273 K [23], and thin films typically exhibit higher resistivity due to grain boundary and surface scattering.

The normal-state resistivity, $\rho_{\mathrm{n}}$ , was taken as the resistivity at 10 K. The transition temperature was defined by the midpoint criterion, $\rho(T_{\mathrm{c}})=0.5\rho_{\mathrm{n}}$ , yielding $T_{\mathrm{c}}=9.24$ K. The transition width was quantified as $\Delta T_{\mathrm{c}}=T_{90}-T_{10}=29$ mK, where $T_{90}$ and $T_{10}$ are the temperatures at which the resistance reaches 90% and 10% of the normal-state value, respectively. RRR, defined as $\rho_{\mathrm{300}}/\rho_{\mathrm{n}}$ , is 5.71. Sample B exhibits a room-temperature resistivity of $\rho_{\mathrm{300}}=24.32\pm 0.07$ µ $\Omega\mathrm{cm}$ , a transition temperature of 9.05 K, a transition width of 41 mK and an RRR of 5.44, showing comparable transport properties between the two deposition runs.

Figure 3 compares the superconducting transition temperatures of samples A and B with values reported for Nb films deposited by direct-current (DC) magnetron sputtering [31, 16, 43, 29] and electron-beam evaporation [27]. Both TLE-grown films exhibit $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ values close to the bulk value of Nb and lie above the reported data at comparable thicknesses. In particular, whereas the reported transition temperature of conventionally deposited Nb films generally decreases appreciably as the thickness approaches the 20–30 nm range, the TLE-grown films retain $T_{\mathrm{c}}>9$ K at a thickness of approximately 22.5 nm. This demonstrates that TLE preserves near-bulk superconducting transition temperatures at lower film thickness compared to prior reports.

To further assess the electrical quality of the TLE-grown films, Fig. 4 compares the room-temperature resistivity, superconducting transition width, and residual-resistivity ratio with literature data. As shown in Figure 4, the measured room-temperature resistivities of the TLE films, $\approx 21.60$ and $24.32$ µ $\Omega\mathrm{cm}$ , fall within the lower range of values reported for sputtered Nb films of comparable thickness. Pinto et al. reported $\rho_{300}=25.6$ µ $\Omega\mathrm{cm}$ for a 25-nm-thick Nb film, while substantial sample-to-sample variations ranging from approximately 20 to 42 $\mu\Omega\mathrm{cm}$ were observed for films in the 20–30 nm thickness range [29]. The room-temperature resistivity of the TLE films is therefore comparable to that of conventionally deposited Nb films.

The superconducting transition widths are compared in Figure 4. Samples A and B, with a thickness of around 22.5 nm, exhibit transition widths of 29 and 41 mK, respectively. These values are comparable to those reported by Pinto et al. [29] and substantially narrower than the values reported by Zhao et al. [43] in a similar thickness range. Pinto et al. [29] reported $\Delta T_{\mathrm{c}}$ values of approximately 15–65 mK for films between 20 and 30 nm, while Zhao et al. [43] observed a rapid increase in the transition width up to approximately 170 mK as the film thickness decreases below 10 nm. Thus, the transition widths of the TLE-deposited samples fall well within the range of characteristics typical of high-quality Nb films. The narrow transition widths further suggest that the near-bulk $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ values are accompanied by spatially uniform superconducting properties [34]. A small $\Delta T_{\mathrm{c}}$ indicates a narrow distribution of local $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ values over the film and is commonly associated with high-quality Nb films [29].

*Figure 5: (a) Upper critical field of sample A as a function of temperature. Red dashed curve shows the best fit by Eq. (2). (b) Coherence length of Nb thin films at different thicknesses. Present work (filled red squares); Ref. 31 (open purple diamonds); Ref. 29 (open yellow squares); Ref. 9 (open brown downward triangles).*

A more pronounced distinction is observed in the residual-resistivity ratio, as shown in Figure 4. The two TLE-grown films exhibit RRR values of 5.71 and 5.44. These values substantially exceed those of the sputtered Nb films reported by Pinto et al. [29] at comparable thicknesses, for which RRR is typically between approximately 2 and 3.5. The values also exceed those reported for high-vacuum electron-beam-evaporated Nb by Morohashi et al. [27], where RRR approaches about 3.2 at a thickness of 100 nm. Since RRR is sensitive to residual defect and impurity scattering, the combination of high RRR and the room-temperature resistivity comparable to that of reported Nb films deposited conventionally suggests a low degree of normal-state disorder in the TLE-grown Nb films.

The temperature dependence of the upper critical field, $\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c2}}(T)$ , of sample A is shown in Figure 5. The upper critical field was determined from resistivity measurements under magnetic fields applied perpendicular to the film plane. For each field, the sample was first stabilized at 12 K, above zero-field $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , and the magnetic field was applied. The sample was then cooled through the full superconducting transition and subsequently heated back to 12 K before the field was changed to the next value. From each resulting resistive transition, $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ was identified using the same 50% resistance criterion employed for the zero-field transition, despite the progressive broadening of the transition with increasing magnetic field. The resulting $\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c2}}(T)$ values were fitted using the empirical expression [19, 29]

$$ \mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c2}}(T)=\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c2}}(0)\frac{1-(T/T_{\mathrm{c}})^{2}}{1+(T/T_{\mathrm{c}})^{2}}, $$

yielding $\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c2}}(0)=1.938\pm 0.004$ T, where the uncertainty represents one standard error estimated from the covariance matrix of the least-squares fit. Using the relation between zero-temperature Ginzburg–Landau (GL) coherence length and the upper critical field,

$$ \mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c2}}(0)=\frac{\Phi_{0}}{2\pi\xi_{\mathrm{GL}}^{2}(0)}, $$

where $\Phi_{0}=2.07\times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{Wb}$ is the magnetic flux quantum, the coherence length was calculated to be $\xi_{\mathrm{GL}}(0)=13.031\pm 0.012$ nm. The uncertainty was propagated from the fitted upper critical field. The same measurement and analysis were applied to sample B, yielding $\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c2}}(0)=1.627\pm 0.005$ T and $\xi_{\mathrm{GL}}(0)=14.224\pm 0.024$ nm. Note that owing to the experimental schedule, the critical-field measurements on sample B were performed approximately two months after deposition. Although the sample was stored in a glovebox during this period, its $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ decreased to 8.78 K at the time of measurement. A possible explanation for this reduction is gradual surface oxidation during storage, which likely reduced the effective film thickness.

Figure 5 compares the coherence lengths of the TLE-grown samples with values reported for Nb thin films in the literature [29, 31, 9]. Because the reported studies employ different criteria for determining $H_{\mathrm{c2}}(T)$ and different models for extrapolating $H_{\mathrm{c2}}(0)$ , this comparison should be regarded as qualitative. Nevertheless, the coherence lengths of the TLE-grown Nb films fall within the range reported for high-quality Nb thin films with thicknesses below 100 nm, providing an additional indication that the superconducting properties of the TLE-grown films are comparable to those obtained using established deposition techniques.

## Discussion

The Nb films deposited by TLE exhibit near-bulk $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ and RRR values approximately 1.5–2.5 times those reported for Nb films of comparable thickness deposited using conventional techniques without substrate heating. Together with the measured surface roughness and other transport and structural properties, these results provide a quantitative picture of the characteristics of Nb thin films deposited by TLE. They complement previous demonstrations of epitaxial superconducting Ta and TiN using thermal laser epitaxy [24, 18].

Building on this work, several technical upgrades to our TLE system would expand the accessible growth conditions and enable synthesis of refractory compounds. Introducing substrate rotation could improve deposition uniformity across the substrate and provide an additional parameter for controlling film texture. Substrate heating, for instance using a CO2-laser substrate-heating system that is installed on our system, would enable in situ high-temperature substrate degassing immediately before growth, reducing the reliance on prolonged room-temperature degassing under vacuum and providing better control over substrate preparation. More importantly, active substrate heating would extend TLE beyond unheated deposition and enable systematic studies of temperature-dependent nucleation, texture, and epitaxial growth phenomena. The integration of an N2 plasma source would further introduce a controllable source of reactive nitrogen, extending the system toward reactive growth of refractory nitrides and carbonitrides. Together, these upgrades would make the system a more versatile platform for investigating the growth of refractory metals and other high-temperature materials.

As a potential direction for future work, the addition of substrate heating could be used to further explore the superconducting properties of TLE-grown Nb. In the supplemental measurements of Glotzer et al., elemental Nb grown on sapphire at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by electron-beam evaporation exhibits a superconducting transition near 9.6 K, exceeding the bulk value of approximately 9.25 K [15]. Given that the Nb films demonstrated here already reach a near-bulk $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ without substrate heating, the introduction of substrate temperature as an additional growth parameter may provide a route toward further optimization of the Nb film structure and potentially allow superconducting transition temperatures to exceed those obtained in the present unheated growth conditions.

Beyond Nb and superconducting materials, the combination of controlled substrate heating and a reactive N2 plasma source would also open access to a broader class of refractory compounds. A future direction for TLE is the controlled synthesis of binary and ternary transition-metal carbides and nitrides, particularly Zr- and Hf-based systems, to investigate how surface thermodynamics, growth kinetics, impurities, and vapor fluxes govern thin-film phase formation and microstructure. Although these materials have been studied extensively in bulk, uncertainties remain in their phase equilibria and thermophysical properties, while thin-film growth introduces additional phenomena through surface energies, kinetic limitations, and strain [36]. TLE could therefore provide a useful platform for systematically exploring both equilibrium and metastable phases under well-controlled conditions compared to sputtering or other PVD techniques. This direction is particularly interesting for the Hf–C–N system, where first-principles calculations predict carbonitride compositions with the highest melting temperatures among all known materials [17].

## Conclusion

In summary, superconducting Nb thin films were deposited on c-plane sapphire by TLE. The films exhibited smooth surfaces, well-defined crystalline textures, and reproducible superconducting properties, with the highest $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ of 9.24 K obtained for a $22.47\pm 0.05$ nm-thick film. The TLE-grown films exhibit near-bulk superconducting transition temperatures and high RRR values relative to previous reports. These results indicate that TLE can deposit high-quality superconducting Nb thin films and motivate further studies of a broader range of deposition conditions and refractory compounds.

# High-field charge transport and noise in p-Si from first principles

**Authors:** David S. Catherall Affiliation: Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA Austin J. Minnich Email: aminnich@caltech.edu Affiliation: Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA

## Abstract

The parameter-free computation of charge transport properties of semiconductors is now routine owing to advances in the ab-initio description of the electron-phonon interaction. Many studies focus on the low-field regime in which the carrier temperature equals the lattice temperature and the current power spectral density (PSD) is proportional to the mobility. The calculation of high-field transport and noise properties offers a stricter test of the theory as these relations no longer hold, yet few such calculations have been reported. Here, we compute the high-field mobility and PSD of hot holes in silicon from first principles at temperatures of 77 and 300 K and electric fields up to 20 kV cm-1 along various crystallographic axes. We find that the calculations quantitatively reproduce experimental trends including the anisotropy and electric-field dependence of hole mobility and PSD. The experimentally observed rapid variation of energy relaxation time with electric field at cryogenic temperatures is also correctly predicted. However, as in low-field studies, absolute quantitative agreement is in general lacking, a discrepancy that has been attributed to inaccuracies in the calculated valence band structure. Our work highlights the use of high-field transport and noise properties as a rigorous test of the theory of electron-phonon interactions in semiconductors.

## I Introduction

The calculation of semiconductor charge transport properties from first principles is of fundamental interest as a test of the theory of electron-phonon interactions and of practical interest for device applications [1, 2]. Recent advances in the ab-initio description of electron-phonon interactions have enabled the calculation of phonon-limited mobility without adjustable parameters using density functional theory (DFT), density functional perturbation theory (DFPT), Wannier interpolation to fine grids needed for transport calculations, and the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) [3, 2]. Implementations of this approach are now available in various software packages [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], and have been applied to calculate low-field properties in a number of materials such as Si [9, 10, 11] and GaAs [11, 12, 13], 2D materials including graphene [14, 15, 16, 17] and MoS2 [17, 9, 16, 18, 19], and others [1]. The approach continues to develop, with advances in the ab-initio description of two-phonon scattering [20], neutral and ionized impurity scattering [21, 22], quadrupole interactions [23, 24], and others [25, 26].

In addition to low-field transport, calculations of high-field transport and noise properties are of particular interest as additional phenomena occur that are not present in the low-field regime. For instance, at sufficiently large electric fields the conductivity exhibits a field dependence and an anisotropy even in cubic crystals [27]. Furthermore, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem is not valid in non-equilibrium systems, meaning that fluctuation and noise properties such as the current power spectral density contain qualitatively distinct information about transport processes not available from mean properties such as mobility [28, 29, 30, 31]. In non-polar semiconductors, these high-field effects were first experimentally observed as a departure from Ohm’s law in Ge and Si [32, 33, 34, 35]. Development of the time-of-flight (TOF) technique allowed the hot-carrier drift velocity to be measured, revealing high-field effects including anisotropy, drift velocity saturation, and negative differential conductivity in n-Si [36] and p-Si [37, 38, 39, 40]. The TOF technique has also been used to measure the diffusion coefficient [41, 42, 43, 44]. The contemporaneous development of measurements of the spectral noise power of current fluctuations also allowed for the determination of noise temperature [45, 46] and diffusion coefficient [43, 47, 44, 48] using the fluctuation-diffusion relation [49]. Measurements at cryogenic temperatures have also found that non-Ohmic behaviour becomes more apparent as temperature decreases [50, 51, 52].

Various theoretical and numerical methods have been employed to interpret these measurements in terms of microscopic transport processes [53, 54, 55, 56, 42]. In particular, high-field transport phenomena in p-Si have been primarily studied via Monte Carlo (MC) methods, which have investigated both steady-state [57, 58, 59, 60] and fluctuation phenomena [43, 40, 61]. While these and other works employed semi-empirical approximations for the band structure and scattering rates, recent works have employed full-band calculations which partially relax prior approximations [62, 63, 64, 65, 66] and applied them to various materials including p-Si [67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72]. However, no MC study on p-Si has employed a fully ab-initio band structure and scattering rates.

The fully ab-initio treatment of electron-phonon scattering [2, 73] has recently been used to calculate low-field hole properties in silicon [74, 75]. These works found that ab-initio calculations with one-phonon scattering, spin-orbit coupling, and the relaxation time approximation is generally adequate to predict the low-field mobility. Overestimates of the mobility of around 30% were attributed to inaccuracies in the DFT valence band structure. Recent works have extended the ab-initio method to study high-field transport phenomena and noise [76, 77, 78]. High-field transport calculations offer a stricter test of the theory because band anisotropy, intervalley and interband scattering, and energy relaxation take on increased importance [79, 53, 29, 80]. Additionally, the full solution to the BTE is necessary at high fields [81, 76]. However, recent methods for the ab-initio treatment of high-field transport [77, 76, 78] have not yet been applied to p-type semiconductors.

Here, we report ab-initio calculations of high-field mobility and current PSD of hot holes in p-Si at electric fields up to 20 and 12 kV cm-1 and temperatures of 300 and 77 K. We find that the calculated properties quantitatively reproduce the trends of high-field transport including the electric field-dependence and anisotropy of the mobility and PSD, and the rapid variation of energy relaxation time with electric field at cryogenic temperatures. We find that the absolute transport properties are uniformly overestimated by around $\sim 25$ %, consistent with the origin being inaccuracies in the valence band structure. Our work demonstrates the utility of the first-principles calculations of high-field transport and fluctuation properties of semiconductors as a stringent test of the theory of electron-phonon interactions.

## II Theory and numerical methods

The details of the method used in this work have been described previously [76, 77]. In summary, high-field transport and noise properties are calculated by solving the Boltzmann transport equation with the electronic states, phonon dispersion, and electron-phonon collision matrix computed from first principles. In a homogeneous system in which carriers are subjected to an electric field, the BTE is given by:

$$ {\frac{q\mathbf{E}}{\hbar}\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}f_{\lambda}=-\Theta_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}\Delta f_{\lambda^{\prime}}} $$

where $q$ is the carrier charge, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field vector, and $f_{\lambda}$ is the carrier occupation function indexed by $\lambda$ which represents the combined indices of band $n$ and wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ . Here, $\Theta_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}$ is the linearized collision integral as given by Eq. 3 of Ref. [76]. The collision integral depends on the phonon populations which may be perturbed by Joule heating, an effect known as the hot phonon effect [82, 83]. Owing to the small free carrier densities in the relevant experiments ( $\lesssim 10^{14}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ ), this effect may be neglected as the non-equilibrium phonon generation rate is too small to affect hole transport properties.

Equation 1 can be expressed as a linear system of equations as described in Sec. II.A. of Ref. [76]. The only necessary modification for the present work is a change of sign for the term implementing the momentum-space derivative to account for the charge carriers being holes. The BTE then takes the form:

$$ {\sum_{\lambda^{\prime}}\Lambda_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}\Delta f_{\lambda^{\prime}}=\sum_{\gamma}\frac{e\mathrm{E}_{\gamma}}{k_{B}T}v_{\lambda,\gamma}f^{0}_{\lambda}} $$

where $\mathrm{E}_{\gamma}$ and $v_{\lambda,\gamma}$ are the electric field strength and hole velocity in the $\gamma$ Cartesian axis, and $\Delta f_{\lambda}$ is the perturbation to the equilibrium distribution function $f^{0}_{\lambda}$ . The relaxation operator $\Lambda_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}$ is defined as:

$$ {\Lambda_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}=\Theta_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}-\sum_{\gamma}\frac{e\mathrm{E}_{\gamma}}{\hbar}D_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime},\gamma}} $$

where $D_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime},\gamma}$ is the finite difference matrix representation of the momentum-space derivative. The solution to the linear system, $\Delta f_{\lambda}$ , can be used to calculate various observables. For instance, the mobility is given as [9]:

$$ {\mu_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{E})=\frac{2e^{2}}{k_{B}T\mathcal{V}}\sum_{\lambda}v_{\lambda,\alpha}\sum_{\lambda^{\prime}}\Lambda^{-1}_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}\left(v_{\lambda^{\prime},\beta}f^{0}_{\lambda^{\prime}}\right)} $$

where $\mathcal{V}$ is the supercell volume, $\alpha$ is the direction along which the current is measured, and $\beta$ is the direction along which the electric field is applied. In addition to mobility, which represents a mean characteristic of the steady-state distribution, the current power spectral density (PSD), which quantifies the random fluctuations of carriers about the non-equilibrium steady-state distribution, may be calculated using the BTE. As given in Sec. II.B. of Ref. [76], the PSD can be computed as:

$$ {S_{j_{\alpha}j_{\beta}}(\mathbf{E},\omega)=2\left(\frac{2e}{\mathcal{V}}\right)^{2}\mathfrak{R}\left[\sum_{\lambda}v_{\lambda,\alpha}\sum_{\lambda^{\prime}}\left(i\omega\mathbb{I}+\Lambda\right)_{\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}^{-1}\left(f^{s}_{\lambda^{\prime}}\left(v_{\lambda^{\prime},\beta}-V_{\beta}\right)\right)\right]} $$

where $\omega$ is the angular frequency, $\mathbb{I}$ is the identity matrix, and $f^{s}_{\lambda}=f^{0}_{\lambda}+\Delta f_{\lambda}$ is the steady distribution. Here, $V_{\beta}$ is the drift velocity, given by:

$$ {V_{\beta}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\lambda}v_{\lambda,\beta}f^{s}_{\lambda}} $$

where $N=\sum_{\lambda}f_{\lambda}$ is the number of holes in the Brillouin zone.

The numerical methods are identical to those in Refs. [76, 77]. The calculation of electronic structure and electron-phonon matrix elements are performed with Quantum Espresso [84, 85] using a coarse 8 $\times$ 8 $\times$ 8 grid, wave function energy cutoff of 60 Ryd, and a lattice constant of 5.430 Å. The spin-orbit interaction is included. The interpolation to fine grids is performed using PERTURBO [7]. The BTE, formulated as a linear system of equations, is solved using the GMRES algorithm [86]. Observables are calculated using a Brillouin zone sum. Transport and noise properties are calculated for lattice temperatures of 300 K and 77 K, with carrier densities of 1016 cm-3 and 1014 cm-3, maximum energy of 192 meV and 92 meV, Gaussian smearing parameters of 5 meV and 2.5 meV, and grid densities of 1203 and 1803, respectively. Increasing the grid densities to 1303 and 1903, respectively, resulted in less than a 1% change in mobility and PSD with the exception of the 77 K PSD, which exhibited a 3% change at the highest fields. These convergence results are in agreement with a recent low-field study [74]. Only the heavy and light valence bands were included in the calculations presented as the split-off band was found to contribute negligibly to all quantities while considerably increasing computational costs. In the following results, normalized computed quantities are shown relative to their value at 1 V cm-1. The error between calculations and experiments for arbitrary property $y$ as a function of some parameter is defined as $||y_{exp}-y_{calc}||_{2}\,/\,||y_{exp}||_{2}$ . The anisotropy for a property along different crystallographic directions is defined at one parameter value $x$ for direction $\alpha$ as $|{y(x)}_{[100]}-{y(x)}_{\alpha}|\,/\,|{y(x)}_{[100]}|$ .

## III Results

### III.1 Transport

We begin by examining the electric field dependence of the DC mobility at 300 K. The calculated low-field mobility is 525 cm2 V-1 s-1, overestimated compared to the experimental value of $\sim 450$ cm2 V-1 s-1 [43, 51]. We find that calculations yield the same overestimate at all fields, so the mobilities have been normalized to facilitate the comparison of trends; computed data are normalized to the calculated low-field mobility, while experimental data are normalized to the low-field mobility measured by Ref. [43] ( $450$ cm2 V-1 s-1).

The calculated DC mobility versus electric field in various crystallographic axes is shown in Fig. 1 along with experimental data from Refs. [51, 43]. At low fields $\lesssim 1$ kV cm-1, the mobility is nearly constant as expected in the Ohmic regime. At fields $\gtrsim 1$ kV cm-1, the mobility decreases with increasing field. We find the normalized mobilities are in quantitative agreement with experiment, with errors of only 2.5% and 5.4% for the $[100]$ and $[111]$ directions, respectively (compared to Ref. [51]). Additional data can be found in Ref. [39], which is not shown but is also in similar agreement. There is a minor discrepancy in the onset of anisotropy, which occurs at fields $\sim 80\%$ lower than predicted by experiment for the $[111]$ direction. However, the anisotropy at high fields is in good agreement with experiment; at 20 kV cm-1 the $[111]$ anisotropy is 13% and 11% for the calculations and measurements, respectively. It was also found that the properties along the $[110]$ and $[111]$ directions are degenerate at all fields, in agreement with data from Ref. [39].

*Figure 1: (a) Normalized DC mobility versus electric field at 300 K. Calculated data normalized to their values at 1 V cm-1, experimental data normalized to the low field value of Ref. [43] ( $450$ cm2 V-1 s-1). Calculated data shown for electric fields in various crystallographic axes including $[100]$ (solid red line) and $[111]$ (dotted blue line). Experimental data shown from Canali et al. [51] ( $[100]$ as red circles, $[111]$ as blue circles), and Nava et al. [43] ( $[111]$ as blue squares). (b) Hole distribution function versus energy ( $f_{\epsilon}$ ), from the valence band maximum at 300 K for electric fields of 1 kV cm-1(solid light blue line), 10 kV cm-1 (dashed orange line), and 20 kV cm-1 (dotted magenta line) applied along the $[100]$ crystallographic axis. The equilibrium distribution is shown as a dashed black line. The distribution function was calculated using kernel density estimation. Inset: deviation from the equilibrium distribution function $\Delta f_{\epsilon}=f_{\epsilon}-f^{0}_{\epsilon}$ . The redistribution of holes to higher energies with increased field strength is evident, leading to the decrease in mobility in (a).*

The decrease in mobility with increasing field can be be attributed to the heating of the holes owing to their finite energy relaxation time. Hole scattering rates increase with energy (see Fig. 6b of Ref. [74]). Thus, the mobility decreases as holes are heated by the applied electric field. To illustrate this point, we computed the hole distribution versus energy at various electric fields in Fig. 1. At low fields ( $\lesssim 3$ kV cm-1), the steady-state distribution of holes coincides with the thermal distribution, and $\Delta f_{\epsilon}\approx 0$ . At higher fields, $\Delta f_{\epsilon}$ becomes non-negligible and the steady-state distribution $f_{\epsilon}$ is shifted to higher energies, ultimately leading to a nonlinear response between drift velocity and electric field.

Next, we show the mobility versus electric field at 77 K in Fig. 2. Data from Refs. [52, 50] were originally reported in normalized form, and are thus presented separately from Ref. [39] for which the absolute high-field mobility was reported but not the low-field mobility, complicating the normalization. At this temperature the low-field mobility is again overestimated, with a value of 12300 cm2 V-1 s-1 compared to the experimental value of $\sim 9800$ cm2 V-1 s-1 [39, 87]. Mobility versus field at 77 K for Refs. [52, 50] are presented in Fig. 2, along with calculations. Quantitative agreement with experiment is observed from 0 – 0.6 kV cm-1. Above this field there is a minor discrepancy in the $[100]$ direction from Ref. [52], but other data remain in agreement with calculations. The overall error between calculations in the $[100]$ direction with data from Ref. [52] is 3.6%.

*Figure 2: (a) Normalized DC mobility versus electric field at 77 K. Calculated data shown for electric fields along the crystallographic axes $[100]$ (solid red line) and $[111]$ (dotted blue line). Calculated data normalized to their values at 1 V cm-1. Experimental data shown from Tschulena [52] ( $[100]$ red triangles, $[111]$ blue triangles) and Asche et al. [50] ( $[111]$ blue squares). (b) Same as (a) but for data from Ref. [39] ( $[100]$ red circles, $[111]$ blue circles), normalized to 9800 cm2 V-1 s-1.*

Experimental data from Ref. [39], which do not reach the Ohmic regime, have been normalized to 9800 cm2 V-1 s-1 and are presented in Fig. 2 along with calculated data. While the computed $[111]$ anisotropy is once again in good quantitative agreement, being 20% (15%) for calculations (measurements) at 12 kV cm-1, the mobility-field values only agree qualitatively, with an error of $\sim$ 12.5% in all crystallographic directions. At 77 K, the $[110]$ mobility is not degenerate with the $[111]$ mobility, with 23 % (29%) calculated (measured) anisotropy, but data for this field direction is omitted for clarity. It should be noted, however, that comparing experimental data from both figures in the region of 0.1–0.7 kV cm-1, the data from Refs. [52, 50] agree quantitatively with the calculations while the data from Ref. [39] do not. Some inconsistency therefore exists between measurements in these references, and the appropriate reference for comparison is not presently clear.

### III.2 Noise

We next examine the PSD in the low-frequency limit, defined as frequencies for which $\omega\tau\ll 1$ . Here, $\tau$ is a characteristic relaxation time of energy, momentum, or similar parameter. In this limit, the current PSD is proportional to the diffusion coefficient through the fluctuation-diffusion relation (see Eqn. 2.49 of Ref. [49]). Experimentally, the diffusion coefficient has been obtained by the TOF method [79] and from low-frequency noise measurements [43, 48]. We calculate the diffusion coefficient through the current PSD, which was computed at 1 GHz to obtain the low-frequency value; negligible differences were observed between 1 GHz and 100 MHz.

The hole diffusion coefficient versus electric field at 300 K is shown in Fig. 3. Experimental measurements from TOF and noise data from Ref. [43] are also shown normalized to the equilibrium value reported by the same study (11.6 cm2 s-1). The calculations are in reasonable quantitative agreement with experiment, with an error of 5.5%, although the data from noise measurements are much closer to calculations, with an error of only 2.5%. At 300 K, comparing Figs. 1 and 3, we observe that the decrease in diffusion coefficient with increasing electric field follows the same trend as that of the mobility. This result is expected as the system remains in the warm carrier regime for all fields considered. Specifically, at the highest field presented here, the mean energy of the steady-state distribution is greater than that of the equilibrium distribution by $\sim 10\%$ , indicating that the steady-state distribution remains close to the equilibrium distribution. In this case, the fluctuation-dissipation relation remains approximately valid [76], so $D(\mathbf{E})\approx\mu(\mathbf{E})k_{B}T/q$ according to the Einstein relation.

*Figure 3: (a) Normalized hole diffusion coefficient versus electric field at 300 K. Calculated data normalized to their values at 1 V cm-1. Calculated data shown for electric fields applied in the crystallographic axes $[100]$ (solid red line) and $[111]$ (dotted blue line). Experimental data shown from Nava et al. [43] ( $[111]$ , noise measurements as blue circles, TOF measurements as blue triangles) and normalized to 11.6 cm2 s-1. (b) Same as (a) at 77 K. Experimental data shown from Reggiani et al. [88] ( $[100]$ as red squares, $[111]$ as blue squares) and Gasquet et al. [48] ( $[111]$ as blue crosses).*

At 77 K and high fields ( $\gtrsim 0.1$ kV cm-1), holes enter the hot carrier regime, with mean energies exceeding the equilibrium value by up to 200% at 6 kV cm-1. Thus, in contrast to the 300 K case, it is expected that the mobility and diffusion coefficient exhibit distinct dependencies on electric field. We present the diffusion coefficient versus field at 77 K in Fig. 3. Experimental data have been normalized to the approximate low-field diffusion coefficient obtained from the Einstein relationship assuming 9800 cm2 V-1 s-1 as the low-field mobility (yielding 65 cm2 s-1). The calculations predict an initial decrease, followed by a plateau around $\sim 0.5$ kV cm-1, and a subsequent decrease. This trend has been previously attributed to the rapid increase in energy relaxation rate once optical phonon emission becomes possible (see Ref. [89] and p.70 of Ref. [29]). The differing trends of mobility and diffusion coefficient highlight the failure of the Einstein relationship and hence the utility of calculating both steady-state and fluctuation properties for high fields.

The 77 K diffusion coefficient calculations exhibit qualitative agreement with experiment, but discrepancies are clearly present. At 3 kV cm-1, the calculated (experimental) $[111]$ anisotropy is 26% (39%), indicating the anisotropy has been reasonably captured. However, the plateau feature in the calculation is not evident in the data. We note that experimental details are not available for data from Ref. [88], and data from both Refs. [88, 48], obtained from TOF measurements, have uncertainties on the order of 25% [90]. Comparison of the trends is therefore challenging considering the uncertainties in experiment.

### III.3 Energy relaxation time

At low temperatures the mechanisms by which carriers lose energy depend on the electric field strength. At low fields, scattering is dominated by acoustic phonons because holes lack sufficient energy to emit optical phonons, and the energy relaxation time (ERT) achieves its maximum value with little dependence on field strength. At high fields, the carriers are heated to energies sufficient to emit optical phonons, and the ERT decreases by orders of magnitude [91]. Experimentally, the field-dependent ERT has been estimated by measuring the transverse noise temperature and using a phenomenological energy balance equation as:

$$ \tau_{\epsilon}(\mathrm{E})=\frac{3k_{B}}{2e}\frac{\left(T^{n}_{\perp}-T_{0}\right)}{\mu\mathrm{E}^{2}} $$

where $\mu$ is the DC mobility at electric field $E$ , $T^{n}_{\perp}$ is the transverse noise temperature, and $T_{0}$ is the lattice temperature (see Sec. 9.2 of [29] or Sec. 4.5 of Ref. [53]). However, computationally the energy relaxation time can be attained more straightforwardly though the energy PSD; this property follows the form of the current PSD in Eq. 5 but with the quantity of interest being energy instead of velocity, as follows:

$$ S_{\epsilon\epsilon}(\mathbf{E},\omega)=2\left(\frac{2}{\mathcal{V}}\right)^{2}\mathfrak{R}\left[\sum_{\lambda}\epsilon_{\lambda}\sum_{\lambda^{\prime}}\left((i\omega\mathbb{I}+\Lambda)^{-1}_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}(f^{s}_{\lambda^{\prime}}(\epsilon_{\lambda^{\prime}}-\mathcal{E}))\right)\right] $$

where $\epsilon_{\lambda}$ is the energy of a hole relative to the energy at the valence band maximum, and $\mathcal{E}$ is the mean energy given by:

$$ {\mathcal{E}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\lambda}\epsilon_{\lambda}f^{s}_{\lambda}} $$

A representative calculated energy PSD is shown in Fig. 3b of Ref. [76]. The ERT is then obtained from a Lorentzian fit of the computed energy PSD [29]:

$$ S_{\epsilon\epsilon}(\mathbf{E},\omega)=\frac{S_{\epsilon\epsilon}(\mathbf{E},0)}{1+\left(\omega\tau_{\epsilon}\right)^{2}} $$

*Figure 4: Hole energy relaxation time versus electric field applied in the $[110]$ direction at 77 K from calculation (dashed light blue line) and experiment (black circles, Ref. [47]). Also shown is the equilibrium (zero field) value of $\tau_{\epsilon}$ measured by Hess and Seeger [92] (orange arrow).*

We compare our ERT calculations to the experimental data reported in Ref. [47]. The experimental and calculated ERT are shown in Fig. 4. We find the equilibrium energy relaxation time at zero electric field to be within $\sim 30$ % of the value obtained from [92]. High-field calculations are also in quantitative agreement with experiment considering the experimental uncertainty. As expected, the ERT shows a rapid decrease with field once optical phonon emission becomes possible around $\sim 0.1$ kV cm-1, consistent with the start of the diffusion coefficient plateau in Fig. 3.

## IV Discussion

The quantitative agreement of most normalized transport properties with experiment indicates that momentum and energy relaxation scattering processes of hot holes in Si are adequately described by the lowest level of pertubation theory in the electron-phonon interactions used in prior works for non-polar semiconductors [9, 75, 74]. Additionally, the relative differences in curvature of the valence band structure in different crystallographic directions appear to be captured as evidenced by the agreement of the high-field anisotropy. However, as in low-field studies [75, 74], absolute transport properties are uniformly overestimated by $\sim 25$ % at all fields. The low-field mobility overestimate has previously been attributed to an inaccurate valence band structure [75]. Examination of our valence band structure and that of Ref. [75] (Fig. 2b, ‘SOC’ case) indicates that the two are in quantitative agreement to within 5% as measured by the average root-mean square difference of the dispersions, excepting the heavy holes in the $\Gamma-\mathrm{K}$ direction which exhibit a $\sim 20$ % heavier mass compared to those in Ref. [75]. This difference is several times smaller than the difference with the dispersion which yields the experimental mobility. Our computed scattering rates are in similar quantitative agreement with prior literature, with the values falling within the range of those reported in Fig. 6b of Ref. [74]. Therefore, our results support the findings from low-field studies in which the overestimated transport properties were attributed to inaccuracies in the DFT valence band structure.

Future work may provide additional tests of the theory by using the present formalism to compute other transport properties, including the high-field drift velocity at $T<40$ K for which a plateau in drift velocity versus electric field is observed; [39] and the microwave PSD, which exhibits a non-monotonic feature at 77 K [47]. A superlinear current-voltage characteristic has also been reported at for p-Si at 77 K under uniaxial stress [93], which has been attributed to the shifting of carriers to the light holes due to strain-induced splitting of the heavy and light-hole bands at $\mathbf{k}=0$ . This phenomenon makes an investigation of the transport and noise properties of strained p-Si of distinct interest.

## V Summary

We have presented a study of hot hole transport and noise in silicon. We find that the ab-initio calculations quantitatively reproduce various experimental trends up to 20 kV cm-1. Absolute properties are generally overestimated by $\sim 25$ %, consistent with prior low-field studies. This agreement may be improved by the use of a more accurate valence band structure. This work highlights the use of high-field transport and noise properties as a rigorous test of the theory of electron-phonon interactions in semiconductors.
